# Depictio Documentation

> Documentation for Depictio

Depictio turns bioinformatics pipeline results into interactive, shareable dashboards: a FastAPI backend, a React viewer, MongoDB, S3 storage and a Python CLI that ingests results. Every CLI command and option is also available as JSON at depictio-cli/cli-reference.json.


# Start

# 

A modern open-source platform that transforms bioinformatics workflow outputs into interactive dashboards.\
Build, share, and explore data visualizations with or without writing code.

Bioinformatics pipelines produce more output than anyone reads. Depictio turns that output into dashboards you can hand to a collaborator, from any execution engine: Nextflow, Snakemake, Galaxy or a shell script.

## Workflow Ecosystem

Connect with standardized bioinformatics workflows from various platforms.

### Card

Overview styles

- One metric per card: count, sum, average, median, unique values and more
- A secondary view shows its shape: donut, box plot, sparkline, histogram, gauge
- Follows every filter on the dashboard

[Card docs →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/components/#card-components)

### Table

Abundance

- AG Grid with server-side paging, so large tables stay fast
- Sort and filter by column, export to CSV
- Selecting rows filters the dashboard

[Table docs →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/components/#table-components)

### Interactive

Linked filters Filters in action Filter panel

- Range slider, slider, multi-select, date picker, segmented control, text search
- Each filter applies to every linked component
- Grouped in a filter panel at the side of the dashboard

[Interactive docs →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/components/#interactive-components)

**Plots**Status heatmapCoverage linesInsert sizeStacked barsVariant effects **Table**General stats

[MultiQC docs →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/components/#multiqc-components)

### Map

Sampling sites

- Tile maps from latitude and longitude columns, no API key
- A click or a lasso on the sites filters the dashboard

[Map docs →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/components/#map-components)

### Genome browser

Tracks Navigator

- JBrowse 2 inside the dashboard, no browser server to run, bound to a manifest of track files: bigWig, BAM, VCF, BED, GFF
- GenomeSpy lanes (the Navigator) show every library along the genome, here coloured by time point: brush a region and the browser opens on it
- The browser's window is drawn as a band on the lanes, and a click on a feature filters the dashboard on its sample
- Filters pick the tracks and frame the locus

[Genome browser docs →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/genome-browser/index.md)

### Text

Overview Study & run

- Markdown blocks between the plots
- Say what the dashboard answers and how to read it
- Values computed from the data and the run parameters, kept up to date

[Text docs →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/components/#text-components)

Cell Painting

- Image galleries served from S3-compatible storage
- Filtered by the dashboard's interactive components
- Click a thumbnail for the full-size image

## Key Features

From the command line that reads your pipeline output to the instance an admin runs in production.

### 01Your data, in one place[Projects →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/projects/guide/index.md)

Project & template

### One pipeline, many runs, one place

A project holds the workflows, the data collections and the dashboards that belong together. Declare it in a YAML file or build it from the browser, whichever suits the run. A template turns that declaration into a reusable recipe: one command against a new run of the same pipeline and the whole thing stands up again, project, data collections and dashboards included, ready to read.

[What a project is →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/projects/guide/index.md) [Templates →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/projects/templates/index.md)

New project

### Start from the data

Upload a table, or point Depictio at a folder, a bucket or one file URL and read it in place. It detects the pipeline and offers how to read the folder: flat tables, your own collections with the Project Builder, or a pipeline template. Another run or more tables join the same project later through **Add data**.

[Create a project →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/projects/guide/#create-a-project) [Project Builder →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/projects/guide/#project-builder)

Ingest

### Read where your data lives

Point `depictio ingest` at a finished run, on your laptop or on the cluster where it landed, and it scans the output in place, pushing only the aggregated results, never the raw files. Smaller collections can be added straight from the browser instead. Either way the ingestion report says what was found, what was missing, and the parameters the pipeline ran with.

[Ingest with the CLI →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/depictio-cli/usage/index.md)

Nextflow trigger

### Or let the pipeline ingest itself

Install the trigger once on the machine that runs `nextflow`, and a pipeline that completes is ingested into Depictio on its own, with the template picked from the pipeline's name and version and not a line about Depictio in the pipeline. Install it opt-in with `--default-disabled` and only the runs that pass `--depictio_enabled true` are ingested. A failed run is never ingested, and a problem on Depictio's side leaves the pipeline's exit status alone.

[Nextflow trigger →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/depictio-cli/nextflow-trigger/index.md)

### 02Build the dashboard[Build a dashboard →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/guides/dashboard_creation/index.md)

Build

### Drag, drop, resize

Every component sits on the same grid: drag one anywhere, pull its corner to resize it, and the cards around it move out of the way. Figures, tables, metric cards, image galleries, maps, text, filters and MultiQC panels all behave the same way, and the layout is saved as you go. Nothing here needs code.

[Add a component →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/guides/dashboard_creation/#add-a-component-to-the-dashboard)

Design

### Design your component

Adding a component starts with a choice, and this is the first branch: pick the type, connect it to a data collection, then tune it against a live preview. Axes, colours, layout, cross-filtering, and Code Mode when you want the Plotly figure itself.

[Build a dashboard →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/guides/dashboard_creation/index.md)

Catalog

### Or take one off the shelf

The other branch: the tools catalog recognises which tool produced each output in your project and offers the visualizations that tool is known to support, pre-configured and previewed at the exact grid box the component will occupy.

[Pick from the catalog →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/guides/catalog-picker/index.md)

$ depictio dashboard export \
<id> -o dashboard.yaml

dashboard.yaml

```
components:
  - component_type: card
    data_collection_tag: metadata
    column_name: sample_id
    aggregation: nunique
  - component_type: advanced_viz
    data_collection_tag: ancombc
    viz_kind: volcano
```

$ depictio dashboard import \
dashboard.yaml

YAML

### Or write the dashboard as code

Export any dashboard to a YAML file, review it in a pull request, and import it back into another instance. Sections, filters and every component are plain fields, so a change to a dashboard reviews like any other change.

[Dashboards as YAML →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/yaml-sync/index.md)

Organise

### Room for a real dashboard

Group cards into sections, keep one filter panel across a family of tabs, dock a map beside the data, and inspect any component to see where its numbers come from.

[Sections and tabs →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/dashboards/#sections)

Versions

### Go back to any version, data included

Every change to a dashboard is kept as a version: bookmark one, share it as a read-only preview link, restore it, or bring back a single component. A version also records which commit of each table it drew from, so a past dashboard is shown with the data it showed at the time, and the editor can draw today's layout from earlier data.

[Dashboard and data versions →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/versioning/index.md)

Metadata

### Label samples where you look at them

Open the **Metadata** panel on a dashboard and type labels next to the samplesheet. Each label becomes a group that filters and colours the linked charts, and you can save it back to the table or export it as a sheet.

[Metadata panel →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/metadata-panel/index.md)

### 03Read the science[Components →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/components/index.md)

Visualize

### Plots built for omics

Volcano, Manhattan, UpSet, hierarchical heatmaps, phylogeny, ordination and many more, alongside the usual scatter and bar charts. Each one is an *advanced viz*: you bind it to any table or file whose columns fit it, rather than waiting for the tool that produced the data to draw it for you.

[Every advanced viz →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/components/#advanced-visualizations)

Explore

### Pick a clade, filter everything

Click any internal node and the panel names what you picked: how many tips it holds, how deep it runs, how well the branch is supported, and how those tips break down by taxonomy. Send it through as a filter and every other component on the dashboard narrows to the same samples.

[Phylogeny interaction →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/advanced-visualizations/#phylogenetic)

MultiQC

### Every QC report, in the dashboard

Hand Depictio the MultiQC reports a run produced, from the CLI or straight from the browser, and it aggregates them across every sample and every run; and their data becomes components you place like any other: General Statistics as a table, each module's plot as its own card. Then it goes past what the HTML report can do: join those panels to your sample sheet and to any other collection in the project, and filter all of them at once from your own metadata, from a map, from a date picker, or from any other filter component on the dashboard.

[Working with MultiQC →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/guides/dashboard_creation/#multiqc-integration-v050)

Group

### Slice it, then compare

Lasso points on a plot, pick rows in a table, select a region on the map, or label samples in the **Metadata** panel, and each set becomes a named group. Every figure then colours by the groups at once, or splits into one panel per group, and every card compares them side by side, so treated and control sit together instead of in two browser tabs. A label can be shared on the dashboard, so others see the same comparison.

[Selection groups →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/interactive-selection-filtering/#selection-groups)

Map

### Where the samples came from

Any collection carrying coordinates becomes a map: points, choropleths from your own GeoJSON, or a panel that follows you across every tab. Dock it in the filter rail or float it over the grid, and lasso a region to filter every other component down to the samples inside it, exactly like a dropdown would. Geography stops being a column in a table and becomes a way to ask questions of the run.

[The map panel →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/guides/dashboard_usage/#the-map-panel-v140)

[![](images/guides/whats-new/whats-new-overlay-split.webp)](images/guides/whats-new/whats-new-overlay-split.mp4)

What's new

### *"What's new"* since your last visit

A dashboard remembers what you last saw. **Overlay** rings the new samples on every chart and fades the rest, **Split** sets them beside what you had seen, and **Before | Now** shows one tile as it was. A bell lists what changed while you were away.

[*"What's new"* →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/whats-new/index.md)

Runs

### Compare runs, MultiQC included

The **Runs** tab says what each run produced and what each scan changed. **Compare** opens a dashboard on the new samples, MultiQC figures and General Stats split on them, and a run naming samples already in the project is held back.

[Runs and run comparison →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/runs/index.md) [MultiQC →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/multiqc/index.md)

### 04Run it, extend it[Administration →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/administration/index.md)

Live

### Watch a run as it lands

Opt a project into real-time events and its dashboards hold a WebSocket open. Each time the CLI ingests new data the server broadcasts on that channel and the affected components refresh themselves, with no reload and no polling. A log beside the grid lists the events as they arrive, so you can watch a run fill a dashboard in while it is still running.

[Real-time events →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/guides/realtime-events/index.md)

Operate

### Run your own instance

Depictio is meant to be self-hosted, and the admin panel is built for that: scheduled backups with a retention policy and a restore gated behind validation, tasks, ingestion runs, logs and service health in one view, users and groups, and branding that reaches the whole instance, its name, its logo, its palette, the login screen and the figures it renders.

[Monitoring and tasks →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/administration/monitoring/index.md)

Tools catalog

### Add your tool without writing YAML

And the shelf is yours to stock. Drop one output file, bind its columns in Depictio's own component builder, and Tool Studio writes the catalog entry and opens the pull request for you, so the next person picks what you designed.

[Open Tool Studio →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-tool-studio/)

Migration

### Send a project to another instance

Ask the other instance for an invite code, paste it in the project settings and **Send**. The project lands there with its data, dashboards and images, is imported right away under that code and is served read-only. A ZIP export covers the offline case.

[Move a project →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/administration/migrate/#send-to-another-instance)

## Getting Started

Ready to get started with Depictio?

Python package

### Three commands, from results to dashboard

On a laptop and without Docker: install the package, start the server, then point it at a pipeline's output. The same server runs in Docker Compose or Kubernetes when a team needs it, and a local server [moves to Docker Compose](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/local/#move-to-docker-compose) with its data.

[Python package installation →](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/local/index.md)

```
uv tool install "depictio[local]"
depictio local up
depictio ingest path/to/results
```

# Getting Started with Depictio

This guide will help you get started with Depictio after installation. It covers the basic concepts and workflows to help you begin visualizing your data.

## First Steps

### Installation

If you haven't installed Depictio yet, please refer to the [installation guide](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/index.md) for detailed instructions on how to set up Depictio using Docker Compose, or Helm.

### Accessing the Web Interface

After installation [see the installation guide](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/index.md), you can access the Depictio web interface. If you used Docker Compose or the helm chart with a local setup, the default port is `5080`. Open your web browser and navigate to:

```
http://localhost:5080
```

### Logging In

When you first access Depictio, you'll be prompted to log in with the admin credentials you set before starting the service.

Admin credentials are set at installation time

The initial admin account is created from two environment variables that must be configured **before the first start**:

- `DEPICTIO_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL` — the admin email address
- `DEPICTIO_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD` — the admin password (≥ 16 characters; the server refuses to start if this is absent or too short)

See the [installation configuration guide](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/configuration/index.md) for details on where and how to set these variables.

### Use existing demo data

If you want to explore Depictio with existing demo data, you can use the provided registered iris dataset. A demo dashboard is also already created for you to explore. You can access it by clicking on the **"Iris Dashboard"** on the landing page.

### Register your first project

#### Using the Web Interface

1. **Open Projects**: click **Projects** in the sidebar, then **New project**.
1. **Describe the project**: enter a **Project name** and, optionally, a **Description**. Tick **Make this project public** to let every user see it.
1. **Click Add data**: this opens three steps, **Your data**, **What Depictio found** and **Create**. **Create without data** makes an empty project instead.
1. **Your data**: drop files or folders on **Upload** (CSV, TSV, Parquet, Feather and more, 50 MB each). Or use **Read in place** for a folder, a bucket or one file URL, read where it is.
1. **Check how it is read**: for a folder, **How should Depictio read this folder?** preselects **Flat tables**, **Custom workflows** or **Pipeline template**. A recognised pipeline shows as **Pipeline:** *name* **· Detected**, with **Change** to pick another.
1. **What Depictio found**: check the tables, runs and source Depictio lists. Then click **Create project with N tables**, or **Next** and **Create Project** for a pipeline.

[![](../../images/guides/project-creation/create-project-from-folder.webp)](../../images/guides/project-creation/create-project-from-folder.mp4)

See [Create a project](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/projects/guide/#create-a-project) for every option, and [Add data](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/projects/guide/#add-data) to add tables or runs later.

#### Using the CLI

Use the command-line interface to programmatically manage your Depictio projects and data.

##### Install the CLI

Depictio provides a command-line interface (CLI), the `depictio` command, for managing data ingestion and other tasks. You can install it by following the [CLI installation guide](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/cli/index.md).

##### Create a CLI configuration

Once you have installed the CLI tool, you need a configuration file to interact with Depictio. It holds the address of your Depictio instance and a long-lived token that signs the CLI in as you.

1. Open **Account settings** with your avatar in the top bar, and the **CLI agents** section (v1.17.0+; before, a separate CLI agents page).

1. Click **Add configuration**, give the configuration a name that tells it apart, such as the machine it runs on, and click **Create**.

1. **Save it**: **Download** the file, or **Copy** it, as `~/.depictio/CLI.yaml`. The token is shown only once, and it signs the CLI in as you: keep the file private.

1. **Check the connection** from the machine you saved it on:

   ```
   depictio config check
   ```

The file looks like this (abridged):

```
# ~/.depictio/CLI.yaml
api_base_url: http://localhost:8058
user:
  id: 67658ba033c8b59ad489d7c7
  email: admin@example.com
  is_admin: true
  token:
    access_token: >-
      eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...
    token_type: bearer
    token_lifetime: long-lived
    expire_datetime: '2027-10-12 13:59:59'
    name: laptop
s3_storage:
  service_name: localhost
  service_port: 9000
  external_host: localhost
  external_port: 9000
  external_protocol: http
  bucket: depictio-bucket
  root_user: minio
  root_password: minio123
```

##### Use the CLI tool

You can now use the CLI tool to interact with your Depictio instance. For example, you can list available workflows, upload data collections, and manage your projects. Refer to the [CLI usage documentation](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/depictio-cli/usage/index.md) for detailed usage instructions.

Saved as `~/.depictio/CLI.yaml`, the configuration is the one every command uses by default, so none of them needs `--server`. See [Which server a command uses](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/depictio-cli/usage/#choosing-a-server) for the other ways to name a server.

With no `~/.depictio/CLI.yaml`, the CLI uses the [local server](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/local/index.md): here pipeline results are previewed, then ingested into it:

In that get started guide, you can use the **palmer penguins dataset** to test the CLI tool. This dataset mimics the [palmer penguins dataset](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/), which is a popular dataset for testing data visualization tools.

```
depictio ingest \
    --project-config-path ../api/v1/configs/penguins_dataset/penguins_project.yaml
```

This command will run the CLI tool with the default configuration file and the specified project configuration file. This will create a new project in Depictio with the palmer penguins dataset, including 2 data collections: `physical_features` and `demographic_data`.

Once the data is ingested, the project appears on the **Projects** page. On the project page, **Project settings** holds its **Storage**, **Data refresh**, **Export** and **Create a template** sections, plus **Send** where migration is on.

This will open the dashboard creation modal. Pick the **Palmer Penguins Species Comparison** project, give the dashboard a name, and confirm.

You will land in the editor for the new dashboard, where you can add components. The screenshot below shows the editor against an existing ampliseq dashboard for reference.

Then follow the [dashboard creation guide](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/guides/dashboard_creation/index.md) and [dashboard usage guide](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/guides/dashboard_usage/index.md). These guides will walk you through the process of designing a dashboard, adding components, and configuring interactivity.

# Installation

Run a Depictio server, then install the CLI to load your data into it.

## Quickstart

No git clone, no configuration file.

1. Download

```
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/depictio/depictio/stable/docker-compose.yaml
```

2. Start

```
docker compose up -d
```

Open Depictio

|     | Service      | URL                                               | Notes                               |
| --- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
|     | **Depictio** | [localhost:5080](http://localhost:5080)           | Single-user mode, no login required |
|     | **API docs** | [localhost:8058/docs](http://localhost:8058/docs) | Interactive OpenAPI interface       |

- **Customise credentials**

  ______________________________________________________________________

  Copy `.env.example` to `.env` to change the S3 password.

  [Advanced configuration](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/docker/#advanced-configuration)

- **Try in GitHub Codespaces**

  ______________________________________________________________________

  The Python package in a cloud workspace, with two example projects.

  [Open in Codespaces](https://codespaces.new/depictio/depictio?devcontainer_path=.devcontainer/try/devcontainer.json&quickstart=1)

# Docker Compose Installation

## Quick Start

**Prerequisites**: [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) 20.10+ and [Docker Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/install/) V2.

### Step 1 — Download the compose file

```
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/depictio/depictio/stable/docker-compose.yaml
```

### Step 2 — Start

```
docker compose up -d
```

All services start automatically: MongoDB, Redis, the S3 store (SeaweedFS), backend, viewer, and Celery worker.

Upgrading an install from before v1.12.0?

The bundled S3 store is SeaweedFS instead of MinIO since v1.12.0, and it starts empty: copy your data over first. See [Upgrading to v1.12.0: MinIO → SeaweedFS](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/upgrade/v1.12.0-seaweedfs/#docker-compose).

### Step 3 — Open

| Service  | URL                          | Credentials                    |
| -------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Depictio | <http://localhost:5080>      | *(single-user mode, no login)* |
| API docs | <http://localhost:8058/docs> | —                              |

The S3 store is reachable only inside the Compose network, under the `s3` host name (`minio` still works as an alias), with the credentials `minio` / `minio123` unless you set your own.

That's it!

Depictio starts in **single-user mode** by default — no login, no configuration needed.

Exposing to the network?

Single-user mode disables credential enforcement. Before sharing or deploying beyond localhost, switch to multi-user mode and set strong credentials — see [Custom credentials](#custom-credentials-env-file) below.

______________________________________________________________________

## Advanced Configuration

Everything in this section is **optional**. The Quick Start defaults work for most users.

### Single-user vs Multi-user mode

Depictio ships in **single-user mode** by default: no login, no accounts, one admin user.

| Mode                        | `DEPICTIO_AUTH_SINGLE_USER_MODE` | `DEPICTIO_AUTH_PUBLIC_MODE` | Use case                            |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| **Single-user** *(default)* | `true`                           | `false`                     | Local development, personal use     |
| **Multi-user**              | `false`                          | `false`                     | Team deployment with login          |
| **Public (read-only)**      | `false`                          | `true`                      | Shared dashboards, no auth required |

Switch to multi-user mode and set strong credentials in your `.env`:

```
DEPICTIO_AUTH_SINGLE_USER_MODE=false

# Required in multi-user mode, read on first boot
DEPICTIO_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL=admin@example.com
DEPICTIO_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -base64 24)

# S3 password must be ≥ 8 chars and not a known default
DEPICTIO_S3_ROOT_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -base64 12)
```

Users can then register accounts and log in via the Depictio UI.

Bootstrap is idempotent

The admin account is created only when no non-anonymous admin exists in MongoDB. Changing the bootstrap vars after first boot has no effect.

Expose to the network?

If making Depictio accessible beyond `localhost`, disable single-user mode and change the S3 credentials.

### Custom Credentials (.env file)

To change the S3 credentials or pin a specific version, copy the example file:

```
cp .env.example .env
```

Edit `.env`:

```
# Image tag. Unset: the release the compose file pins; `next` follows main
DEPICTIO_VERSION=1.21.0

# First admin: required in multi-user mode on an empty database (single-user mode seeds its own)
DEPICTIO_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL=admin@example.com
DEPICTIO_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=change-me-strong-password-here

# S3 credentials: in multi-user mode at least 8 chars and not a known default
# Named DEPICTIO_MINIO_* before v1.12.0; the old names still work
DEPICTIO_S3_ROOT_USER=myadmin
DEPICTIO_S3_ROOT_PASSWORD=change-me-strong-password-here
```

Bootstrap is idempotent

The admin account is created only on first boot (when no non-anonymous admin exists in MongoDB). Restarting the container or changing the bootstrap vars afterwards has no effect: use the admin UI to manage credentials.

Full reference

- [Configuration](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/configuration/index.md): what to set first, then by topic
- [Environment Reference](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/env-reference/index.md): every variable, with its default

### External S3

If you already have S3-compatible storage (AWS, NetApp, Ceph, your own MinIO, …), use the compose file without the bundled store:

```
docker compose -f docker-compose/docker-compose.no-minio.yaml up -d
```

Configure your `.env` to point to your existing instance:

```
DEPICTIO_S3_ROOT_USER=your-access-key
DEPICTIO_S3_ROOT_PASSWORD=your-secret-key
DEPICTIO_S3_PUBLIC_URL=https://your-s3-host.example.com
DEPICTIO_S3_EXTERNAL_SERVICE=true
# Optional overrides
DEPICTIO_S3_EXTERNAL_HOST=your-s3-host.example.com
DEPICTIO_S3_EXTERNAL_PORT=9000
DEPICTIO_S3_EXTERNAL_PROTOCOL=https
```

Network Configuration

Set `DEPICTIO_S3_EXTERNAL_SERVICE=true` when the store is outside the Docker Compose network.

The bucket does not have to exist

From **v1.6.0** the server creates `DEPICTIO_S3_BUCKET` at startup when it is missing, then verifies it; an existing bucket is left untouched. See [Required S3 permissions](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/env-reference/#required-s3-permissions).

S3-Compatible Storage

Depictio talks to the store through the S3 API (boto3, s3fs, delta-rs), with no MinIO-specific client. AWS S3, DigitalOcean Spaces, Backblaze B2, and others may work but have not been officially tested.

### Port Configuration

Default ports:

| Service                 | Default port                      |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Frontend (React viewer) | 5080                              |
| Backend API             | 8058, on `127.0.0.1`              |
| MongoDB                 | 27018, inside the Compose network |
| S3 API (SeaweedFS)      | 9000, inside the Compose network  |

The development stack (`docker-compose.dev.yaml`) also publishes the S3 API and the SeaweedFS admin UI on `127.0.0.1`. Move them in `.env` with `S3_PORT` (default `9000`) and `S3_CONSOLE_PORT` (default `9001`), named `MINIO_PORT` and `MINIO_CONSOLE_PORT` before v1.12.0, which still work.

### Development Mode

Reload the API and restart the worker on code changes (telemetry and the walkthrough are off too):

```
DEPICTIO_DEV_MODE=true docker compose up -d
```

Or set `DEPICTIO_DEV_MODE=true` in your `.env` file.

### Celery worker

The `depictio-celery-worker` container always starts: figure previews in the editor, large renders and dashboard thumbnails run on it. Size it in `.env` with `DEPICTIO_CELERY_WORKERS` (default `4` processes); each process holds its own data, so memory sets the limit. When renders are offloaded is set by the `DEPICTIO_CELERY_OFFLOAD_*` variables: see [Celery Task Queue](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/env-reference/#celery-task-queue).

### Ingestion worker (v1.15.0+)

`depictio-ingestion-worker` is a second Celery worker for long ingestion tasks: profiling a table after the CLI has written it, and an ingestion started from a project page. It runs the same image as `depictio-celery-worker` but reads only the `ingestion` queue, so a 20-minute table read never holds up the dashboard editor. It is behind a Compose profile, so `docker compose up -d` alone does not start it:

```
docker compose --profile ingestion up -d
```

| Variable                                | Default | Description                                                                                   |
| --------------------------------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DEPICTIO_INGESTION_WORKER_CONCURRENCY` | `2`     | Tasks run at once. Each holds a table's columns in memory, so memory runs out before CPU does |

Each worker process takes one task at a time and is replaced after 10 tasks. The worker stays idle until one of the two features below is turned on. Both are off by default, and only this Compose file has the worker: the Helm chart and `depictio local up` do not start one.

Set `DEPICTIO_VERSION` before starting the profile

In the v1.15.0 `docker-compose.yaml`, this service defaults to the `1.14.0` image while the others default to `1.15.0`. That image ignores the queue setting, reads the dashboard queue instead of `ingestion`, and never reports healthy. Set `DEPICTIO_VERSION=1.15.0` in `.env`.

Start the worker before turning either feature on. With nothing reading the `ingestion` queue, jobs stay pending.

The server-side ingestions of remote data (v1.16.0+), a project created [from a run folder](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/projects/remote-data/#from-a-run-folder) and a [**Data refresh**](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/usage/projects/remote-data/#refreshing-the-data), run on `depictio-celery-worker` instead: they need neither this worker nor `DEPICTIO_JOBS_ENABLED`.

#### Offloading the table profile

After the CLI writes a Delta table, the server reads it back to profile its columns. On a large table that takes longer than an HTTP request should. With offloading on, the server records the new table version at once and hands the profiling to the ingestion worker. A CLI run with `--async-upsert` then waits for that job instead of a response.

```
# .env
DEPICTIO_JOBS_ENABLED=true
DEPICTIO_INGESTION_ASYNC_DELTATABLE_UPSERT=true
```

```
depictio ingest results/ --server ~/.depictio/CLI.yaml --async-upsert
```

The CLI waits at most `DEPICTIO_INGEST_JOB_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` for each job (`3600`; `0` waits without limit). Without both settings, or against an older server, the server ignores `--async-upsert` and profiles the table within the request. MultiQC collections are never offloaded.

#### Starting an ingestion from the browser

This turns on [**Run ingestion**](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/features/dashboards/#run-ingestion) on project pages. The server then scans and processes the data itself, so it has to see the files: `depictio-backend` checks that the data locations exist, and `depictio-ingestion-worker` reads them.

```
# .env
DEPICTIO_JOBS_ENABLED=true
DEPICTIO_INGESTION_BROWSER_TRIGGER=true
DEPICTIO_INGESTION_ALLOWED_DATA_ROOTS=/data/runs
```

`DEPICTIO_INGESTION_ALLOWED_DATA_ROOTS` takes a comma-separated or JSON list of directories. Every data location, single-file path and image directory of a project must resolve inside one of them, following symlinks, and so must every file the scan registers. It is checked when the button is pressed, again when the worker starts, and on the registered files before they are read. Any signed-in user can create a project and name any path in it, so this list is what keeps an ingestion away from other groups' runs and from the server's own files. Empty, it refuses every ingestion.

Mount the data at the same path in both containers, for example read-only from a `docker-compose.override.yaml` next to `docker-compose.yaml`:

```
services:
  depictio-backend:
    volumes:
      - /srv/sequencing/runs:/data/runs:ro
  depictio-ingestion-worker:
    volumes:
      - /srv/sequencing/runs:/data/runs:ro
```

The projects then name their data under `/data/runs`, the path inside the containers.

On the server, the scan skips any symlink that points outside the directory it walks, so it cannot be led out of the allowed directories. A results directory that Nextflow filled with links into `work/` (`publishDir mode: 'symlink'`) therefore yields no files: publish copies instead, or ingest it with the CLI, which reads a symlinked file wherever it points.

#### Request timeouts

Since v1.15.0 the API server lets a request run for 300 seconds instead of 120, as long as the CLI waits for the server to profile a written table. Before, a slow profile was cut off and the CLI saw a dropped connection rather than an error. The bundled viewer's nginx allows 3600 seconds on API requests. A reverse proxy in front of Depictio should allow at least 300 seconds, or the CLI should use `--async-upsert`.

## Managing Services

| Action                               | Command                                   |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| Stop (preserve data)                 | `docker compose stop`                     |
| Stop and remove containers           | `docker compose down`                     |
| Stop, remove containers **and data** | `docker compose down -v`                  |
| View all logs                        | `docker compose logs -f`                  |
| View one service                     | `docker compose logs -f depictio-backend` |
| Check status                         | `docker compose ps`                       |

______________________________________________________________________

## Troubleshooting

### A container fails to start

```
docker compose logs <service_name>
```

Common causes: port conflict, volume permission error, MongoDB connection failure.

### Cannot connect to services

1. Check containers are running: `docker compose ps`
1. Confirm you are using the correct ports
1. Check for firewall rules blocking the connection

### Data persistence

MongoDB, Redis and the S3 store keep their data in named Docker volumes (`mongo_data`, `redis_data` and `seaweedfs_data`). They persist across `docker compose down`, and `docker compose down -v` deletes them. Before v1.12.0 the store was MinIO, in a `minio_data` volume that SeaweedFS does not read: see [Upgrading to v1.12.0](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/upgrade/v1.12.0-seaweedfs/index.md).

# Kubernetes Installation

Deploy Depictio on a Kubernetes cluster using the official Helm chart.

**Prerequisites**: Kubernetes 1.19+, Helm 3.2.0+, a PV provisioner (if persistence is enabled).

______________________________________________________________________

## Quick Start

### Step 1 — Clone and install

```
git clone https://github.com/depictio/depictio.git
cd depictio

helm install depictio helm-charts/depictio \
  -f helm-charts/depictio/values.yaml \
  -n depictio --create-namespace
```

### Step 2 — Wait for pods

```
kubectl get pods -n depictio --watch
```

All pods should reach `Running` status: backend, viewer, mongo, minio, redis, celery-worker. The `minio` pod runs the S3 store, SeaweedFS since v1.12.0; it keeps its name so that an upgrade reuses the same volume.

Upgrading a release from before v1.12.0?

The bundled store starts empty after the upgrade: export the bucket **before** running `helm upgrade`. See [Upgrading to v1.12.0: MinIO → SeaweedFS](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/upgrade/v1.12.0-seaweedfs/#helm).

### Step 3 — Access Depictio

By default services are `ClusterIP`. Use port-forwarding to access locally:

```
kubectl port-forward -n depictio service/depictio-viewer 5080:5080
```

Then open <http://localhost:5080>.

| Service                 | Port |
| ----------------------- | ---- |
| Frontend (React viewer) | 5080 |
| Backend API             | 8058 |
| S3 API (SeaweedFS)      | 9000 |

The SeaweedFS admin UI is off by default. `s3.adminUI.enabled: true` serves it on `s3.service.adminPort` (`23646`), behind the S3 root credentials.

______________________________________________________________________

## Advanced Configuration

### Custom values file

Create a `my-values.yaml` to override defaults and pass it at install time:

```
helm install depictio helm-charts/depictio \
  -f helm-charts/depictio/values.yaml \
  -f my-values.yaml \
  -n depictio --create-namespace
```

To see all configurable parameters:

```
helm show values helm-charts/depictio
```

### Real-world example (EMBL)

The repository includes the EMBL demo deployment values files as a reference. They demonstrate the **layered approach**: a shared base file overlaid by environment-specific files.

| File                                                                                                                           | Purpose                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| [`values-embl-demo-base.yaml`](https://github.com/depictio/depictio/blob/main/helm-charts/depictio/values-embl-demo-base.yaml) | Shared settings (storage, resources, auth, S3) |
| [`values-embl-demo.yaml`](https://github.com/depictio/depictio/blob/main/helm-charts/depictio/values-embl-demo.yaml)           | Demo overlay (ingress, image tags, replicas)   |
| [`values-embl-demo-dev.yaml`](https://github.com/depictio/depictio/blob/main/helm-charts/depictio/values-embl-demo-dev.yaml)   | Dev overlay (debug flags, reduced resources)   |
| [`values-embl-auth.yaml`](https://github.com/depictio/depictio/blob/main/helm-charts/depictio/values-embl-auth.yaml)           | Multi-user auth + Google OAuth                 |

Usage pattern:

```
helm install depictio helm-charts/depictio \
  -f helm-charts/depictio/values.yaml \
  -f helm-charts/depictio/values-embl-demo-base.yaml \
  -f helm-charts/depictio/values-embl-demo.yaml \
  -n depictio --create-namespace
```

Secrets file

`values-embl-secrets.yaml` is gitignored — it holds the S3 passwords and OAuth secrets that must be created locally. See `values-embl-auth.yaml` for the expected key names.

### Single-user vs Multi-user mode

The chart starts in multi-user mode (sign-in required), unlike the root `docker-compose.yaml`.

```
# my-values.yaml
backend:
  env:
    # DEPICTIO_AUTH_SINGLE_USER_MODE: "true"   # no login, every visitor is the admin
    # DEPICTIO_AUTH_PUBLIC_MODE: "true"        # public read-only with sign-in
```

### S3 credentials

```
# my-values.yaml
secrets:
  s3RootUser: "myadmin"                      # generated when empty
  s3RootPassword: "mysecurepassword"
  bootstrapAdminEmail: "admin@example.org"   # first admin, read on an empty database
  bootstrapAdminPassword: "change-me"
```

These keys were `secrets.minioRootUser` and `secrets.minioRootPassword` before v1.12.0. The old keys, and a `minio:` values block, still work and print a deprecation warning in the upgrade notes. See [Renamed settings](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/upgrade/v1.12.0-seaweedfs/#renamed-settings).

Upgrading from pre-v1.0.0-b1 — rotate the S3 credentials

From **v1.0.0-b1** onwards the S3 root credentials are stored exclusively in a Kubernetes `Secret`. Earlier releases stored them in the `ConfigMap`, which was readable via `kubectl describe` and stored in etcd as plain text.

If you are upgrading from an older release, **rotate your S3 root credentials** after the upgrade:

1. Update `secrets.s3RootUser` and `secrets.s3RootPassword` in your values file (or a sealed secret / external-secrets source).
1. Run `helm upgrade` to apply the new Secret.
1. Restart the store's pod so it picks up the new credentials: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/depictio-minio -n depictio`

### External S3

```
# my-values.yaml
s3:
  enabled: false   # no bundled store (minio.enabled before v1.12.0)

backend:
  env:
    DEPICTIO_S3_PUBLIC_URL: "https://your-s3-host.example.com"
    DEPICTIO_S3_EXTERNAL_SERVICE: "true"
    DEPICTIO_S3_ROOT_USER: "your-access-key"
    DEPICTIO_S3_ROOT_PASSWORD: "your-secret-key"
```

An external S3 is not affected by the move from MinIO to SeaweedFS, and the `DEPICTIO_MINIO_*` names of earlier values files still work.

The bucket does not have to exist

From **v1.6.0** the backend creates `DEPICTIO_S3_BUCKET` at startup when it is missing, then verifies it; an existing bucket is left untouched. See [Required S3 permissions](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/env-reference/#required-s3-permissions).

### Browser access to indexed files (v1.22.0+)

3D structures and file-backed genome tracks are read by the browser. `s3.browserAccess` sets [`DEPICTIO_S3_BROWSER_ACCESS`](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/env-reference/#s3-browser-access) on the backend and the worker:

| Value          | Mode                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `""` (default) | Picked by the chart: `presigned` when it routes the bundled store (`ingress.enabled` or `gateway.enabled`, with `global.domain` set), or when an external store has `DEPICTIO_S3_PUBLIC_URL` in `s3.env`; `proxy` otherwise |
| `presigned`    | Browsers read S3 directly, through presigned URLs                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `proxy`        | The API streams the files: for an S3 store with no public route                                                                                                                                                             |

```
# my-values.yaml
s3:
  browserAccess: proxy   # any other value than "", presigned or proxy fails the install
```

The automatic choice reads `s3.env`, not `backend.env`. With the URL in `backend.env`, as in [External S3](#external-s3) above, it picks `proxy`: set `browserAccess: presigned`, or move `DEPICTIO_S3_PUBLIC_URL` to `s3.env`, if browsers reach the store.

### Ingress

Depictio's Helm chart supports three ingress topologies. Pick based on how your cluster's auth and TLS termination work.

| Topology                       | Toggle                                | When to use                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Single ingress** (default)   | `ingress.enabled: true` only          | Viewer, backend API, and S3 store all share one ingress + annotation set. Right for small/dev clusters or when one OIDC layer covers everything.                                        |
| **Viewer + dedicated backend** | `backend.ingress.separateRoute: true` | Apply different auth annotations (or no auth) on the API. Useful when the API needs a different OIDC scope, or when programmatic clients hit `/depictio/api/*` with mTLS or API tokens. |
| **Viewer + dedicated S3**      | `s3.ingress.separateRoute: true`      | Same idea for the S3 store — typically when it is exposed for direct S3 access from CI runners and shouldn't sit behind the user-facing OIDC.                                           |

You can combine the toggles to get all three ingresses separate.

#### Per-route annotations

Each ingress has its own `annotations` block, applied in isolation:

```
# my-values.yaml
ingress:
  enabled: true
  host: depictio.yourdomain.com
  tls:
    enabled: true
    secretName: depictio-tls
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "100m"
    # OIDC annotations applied to the viewer ingress only

backend:
  ingress:
    separateRoute: true
    inheritDefaultAnnotations: false   # don't copy ingress.annotations
    annotations:
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-method: "BASIC"   # different auth
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "200m"

s3:
  ingress:
    separateRoute: true
    inheritDefaultAnnotations: false
    annotations: {}                     # no auth — restrict at network policy
```

`inheritDefaultAnnotations` controls whether `ingress.annotations` are merged into the per-route ingress. Set `false` when the per-route ingress needs a fundamentally different auth chain.

Network restrictions on dedicated routes

A dedicated S3 or backend ingress with `annotations: {}` is **unauthenticated at the ingress layer**. Restrict access via Kubernetes NetworkPolicies, ingress controller IP whitelisting, or a dedicated private DNS — don't rely on obscurity.

#### Gateway API instead of Ingress (v1.1.4+)

On clusters that have moved to the [Gateway API](https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/), `gateway.enabled: true` emits `HTTPRoute` resources instead of Ingress objects: one for the viewer, one for the API, one for the S3 store. `parentRefs` is the only required key; per-route filters live under `backend.httpRoute` and `s3.httpRoute`, and `gateway.filters` applies to the viewer route alone.

```
# my-values.yaml
ingress:
  enabled: false
gateway:
  enabled: true
  parentRefs:
    - name: nginx-gateway
      namespace: nginx-gateway
```

Gateway API has no equivalent of the `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/*` annotations, so raw nginx config goes through `gateway.snippetsFilter`. Setting `enabled: true` with a list of `snippets` emits a `SnippetsFilter` and wires it into the viewer route. Both keys are ignored while `gateway.enabled` is `false`.

### Init container image pull policy

All init containers must use `pullPolicy: Always`. Capsule and Pod Security Admission (PSA) webhooks on restricted namespaces reject pods whose init containers use `IfNotPresent`, which can leave the release stuck in `Pending`.

```
# my-values.yaml
initContainerImage:
  pullPolicy: Always   # required on clusters with Capsule/PSA admission webhooks

curlInitContainerImage:
  pullPolicy: Always   # same requirement for the curl-based readiness init container
```

These keys map directly to the `initContainerImage.pullPolicy` and `curlInitContainerImage.pullPolicy` fields in `values.yaml`.

### Service link environment variables

Kubernetes injects a block of legacy Docker-link environment variables (`<SVC>_SERVICE_HOST`, `<SVC>_PORT_<port>_TCP_ADDR`, and several more) into every pod, once per service in the namespace. On a busy namespace that set grows large enough to overflow the process argument limit, and the viewer crashloops with `envsubst: Argument list too long` before nginx ever starts.

Since **v1.4.0** the chart sets `enableServiceLinks: false` on every pod it owns, which is the opposite of Kubernetes' own default ([#946](https://github.com/depictio/depictio/pull/946)):

```
# my-values.yaml
enableServiceLinks: false   # chart default; Kubernetes itself defaults to true
```

Depictio's own services address each other by DNS name, so nothing in the application reads those variables. Set it back to `true` only if something else in your deployment does.

What stays injected

`KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` and `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_PORT` are injected by the kubelet regardless of this setting, so in-cluster API clients are unaffected. Pods created by the Percona MongoDB operator are also untouched, since the operator owns those pod specs.

### Celery workers

The Celery worker is enabled by default (`celery.enabled: true`): editor previews, large renders and thumbnails run on it. `DEPICTIO_CELERY_WORKERS` sets its processes (the chart sets `2`); each holds its own data, so size it with the pod's memory limit:

```
# my-values.yaml
celery:
  replicas: 1
  env:
    DEPICTIO_CELERY_WORKERS: "4"
```

No ingestion worker in the chart (v1.15.0)

The chart's worker reads only the default `celery` queue, and the chart has no [ingestion worker](https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/installation/docker/#ingestion-worker) to read the `ingestion` queue. Leave `DEPICTIO_INGESTION_ASYNC_DELTATABLE_UPSERT` and `DEPICTIO_INGESTION_BROWSER_TRIGGER` off on Kubernetes: with either on, the jobs they create are never picked up.

### Pod labels and internet egress (v1.22.0+)

`backend.podLabels` and `celery.podLabels` add labels to the backend and worker pods (the pod template only, never the selector). Both default to the label SciLifeLab Serve reads to allow outbound traffic, which it denies by default:

```
# values.yaml defaults
backend:
  podLabels:
    networking/allow-internet-egress: "true"
celery:
  podLabels:
    networking/allow-internet-egress: "true"
```

The backend dials out for the UCSC track catalogue and genome files, remote tracks, structure lookups, OIDC and migration targets; the worker for remote data at ingestion. The label does nothing on clusters without that policy. To keep a pod off the internet on Serve, set the label to `"false"`: an empty map in an override file does not remove it, since Helm merges maps.

### Resource limits

```
# my-values.yaml
backend:
  resources:
    requests:
      memory: "1Gi"
      cpu: "500m"
    limits:
      memory: "4Gi"
      cpu: "2"

viewer:
  resources:
    requests:
      memory: "512Mi"
      cpu: "250m"
    limits:
      memory: "2Gi"
      cpu: "1"
```

### Google Analytics

```
# my-values.yaml — or use the bundled example
helm upgrade depictio helm-charts/depictio \
  -f helm-charts/depictio/values.yaml \
  -f helm-charts/depictio/examples/values-google-analytics.yaml
```

## Troubleshooting

```
# Check pod status
kubectl get pods -n depictio

# Inspect logs
kubectl logs -n depictio deployment/depictio-backend
kubectl logs -n depictio deployment/depictio-viewer

# Describe a failing pod
kubectl describe pod -n depictio <pod-name>
```

Common causes: insufficient storage class, PVC pending, image pull errors.
